strengths: Originality: Studying image resolution and sample size jointly within a template-deformation model provides a useful statistical perspective. The contribution builds meaningfully on the pattern-recognition and functional-data literature acknowledged in the manuscript.

Significance: The explicit alignment procedure in (18)–(20) and its specialized analysis in Theorem 3.6 provide an interpretable benchmark for classification under scaling, translation, and brightness changes.
Presentation: The manuscript develops the model and algorithms systematically, provides helpful illustrations, and includes extensive proofs that make the intended reasoning inspectable.

Limitations and ethics: Sections 3.2 and 6 appropriately acknowledge background noise, partial visibility, and multiple objects as extensions. These honest qualifications are valuable. No material research-ethics concern is apparent in the theoretical and MNIST-based work.
weaknesses: Soundness—CNN learning guarantee: Equation (27) is not empirical misclassification minimization for labels in {0,1}. Its objective, −∑ᵢ kᵢ1{q₂(Xᵢ)>1/2}, never penalizes false positives. A constant classifier predicting class 1 is therefore a global minimizer for every dataset, yet has test error 1−π. This contradicts Theorem 4.1's vanishing bound for fixed resolution. Equation (94) explicitly asserts the incorrect equivalence with 0–1 ERM. The objective must be corrected and the theorem established for the corrected estimator.

Soundness—inverse-mapping guarantee: The proof of Theorem 3.1 on page 29 applies Lemma A.3 to arbitrary candidate inverses Bᵢ and B, although that lemma guarantees approximation to the normalized template only for an appropriately chosen inverse B*. Because classifier (10) minimizes over all inverse pairs, controlling the correctly chosen pair is insufficient: every incorrect-class pair needs a lower bound. Arbitrary inverse warps can also discard distinguishing image regions in the comparison domain. The central perfect-classification claim consequently lacks a valid proof under the stated assumptions.

Soundness—claimed optimality: Theorem 3.7 constructs indistinguishable pixel observations with raw L2 template separation of order 1/d. It does not establish that the deformation-minimized separation D in (12) or (21) is also of that order. A lower bound on the unaligned distance does not imply a lower bound after minimizing over deformations and brightness. Thus the claimed matching necessity of the separation condition requires an additional argument.

Presentation and mathematical precision: Theorem 4.2 and Lemma 4.3 reference the separation quantity in (21), which concerns axis-wise scaling and translation, whereas the general CNN proof uses (12). These conditions are not interchangeable for rotation or nonlinear deformation classes. The theorem statements and proofs need consistent hypotheses.

Evaluation and significance: Section 5 offers illustrative experiments but does not validate the central resolution or deformation-complexity claims. All experiments fix d=28 and generate samples from one or ten MNIST templates per class. The tested CNN architectures differ from the theoretical construction, and Adam training is not covered by the exact 0–1 ERM analysis. Controlled variation of resolution, separation, and deformation complexity would better establish what the theory explains. The acknowledged noiseless specialization remains useful, but broader implications for practical CNN learning are presently limited.

Reproducibility: Section 5 reports architectures, optimizer, learning rate, and repetition counts, but omits the training loss, epochs, batch size, deformation distributions/ranges, and precise template-selection protocol; no implementation link is supplied. Figure 8 reports medians over 30 repetitions using 100 test images per repetition without variability estimates. These omissions make the empirical findings difficult to reproduce and their reliability difficult to assess.
